10 ABSTRACT: We investigate the eﬀect of high work function

11 contacts in halide perovskite absorber-based photovoltaic

12 devices. Photoemission spectroscopy measurements reveal

13 that band bending is induced in the absorber by the deposition

14 of the high work function molybdenum trioxide (MoO3). We

15 ﬁnd that direct contact between MoO3 and the perovskite

16 leads to a chemical reaction, which diminishes device

17 functionality. Introducing an ultrathin spiro-MeOTAD buﬀer

18 layer prevents the reaction, yet the altered evolution of the

19 energy levels in the methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3)

20 layer at the interface still negatively impacts device perform-

21 ance.

22 KEYWORDS: electronic structures/processes/mechanisms, photoemission spectroscopy, hybrid materials, photovoltaic devices,

23 band oﬀsets, charge carrier transport

24T

he outstanding performance of photovoltaic devices based

25 on hybrid organic−inorganic perovskite absorbers has

26 spurred a ﬂurry of activity aimed at unravelling the fundamental

27 electronic, chemical and physical properties of this class of

28 materials.1−3 In particular, issues related to charge separation

29 and collection, and to the electronic coupling to adjacent

30 charge transport layers, are being extensively investigated.

31 We recently demonstrated that the electronic structure of

32 organic materials used as carrier extraction layers directly aﬀects

33 the device characteristics of both conventional and inverted

34 perovskite solar cells.4,5 Speciﬁcally, a mismatch between the

35 transport levels of the carrier extraction layer and the perovskite

36 active layer would limit the device open circuit voltage (Voc) or

37 introduce an unwanted carrier extraction barrier, and could as

38 well degrade the carrier selectivity by allowing carrier crossover

39 and recombination.4 Such instances were demonstrated with

40 both methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) and bromide

41 (MAPbBr3). In particular, the latter exhibits a large band gap of

42 2.3 eV and high ionization energy (IE) of ∼5.9 eV and thus

43 requires an organic hole-transport layer (HTL) with commen-

44 surable electronic properties.4,6,7 Even in the case of MAPbI3,

45 which exhibits a band gap of ∼1.6 eV and an IE of ∼5.4 eV,

46 signiﬁcant improvements in cell performance were achieved

47 using high ionization energy organic HTLs.8,9

48 The present study focuses on an alternative for hole

49 extraction interlayers, based on high work function metal

50 oxides to enable charge transfer from the perovskite layer into

51 the HTL. In the past few years, the high work function

52 molybdenum trioxide (MoO3) has been successfully used as

53 hole-injection and -extraction material in organic electronics,

54 including solar cells in which it also creates a large built-in

55 voltage.10−13 In these devices, direct transfer of electrons from

56 the very low lying conduction band of the n-type MoO3 57 (electron aﬃnity, EA, of about 6.7 eV) into the highest

58 occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of the donor molecules of

59 the adjacent active layer is responsible for the eﬃcient hole

60 extraction process.10 Moreover, MoO3 interlayers are of

61 considerable interest for the realization of recombination layers

62 in tandem cells based on perovskite subcells.14

63 To date, MoO3 has been considered predominantly as a hole

64 contact on MAPbI3 solar cells on top of the organic HTL, to

65 increase the work function of standard metals like Ag or

66 improve device stability.15,16 Although it was found to improve

67 carrier extraction from the HTL, the considerable spatial

68 separation from the active perovskite layer may have

69 diminished the presumed beneﬁts of the high work function

70 of the oxide, in particular with respect to the built-in voltage

71 and ﬁeld in the active layer. Liu et al. recently investigated

72 chemistry and electronic structure at the MoO3/MAPbI3 73 interface obtained by direct evaporation of the oxide on the

74 perovskite.17 In the present work, we show that the formation

75 of this junction can lead to even more pronounced band

76 bending in the MAPbI3 ﬁlm and to a reduction of the MoO3 to

77 MoO2 at the very interface. We outline, and show initial data

78 for an approach that can mitigate the impact of the oxide/

79 perovskite chemical reaction and improve the chemical integrity

80 of the interface, while preserving the eﬀects of the very high

81 work function overlayer on the built-in ﬁeld. This allows us to

82 identify the impact of the chemically altered interface layer and

83 of the band bending in the perovskite active layer, on device

84 functionality. The MAPbI3 ﬁlm is deposited from solution in a

85 one-step process on top of a thin hole-blocking TiO2 layer,

86 which in turn has been grown on a ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide

87 (FTO)-covered glass substrate by spin-casting from solution.18

88 We ﬁnd the performance of devices comprising a direct contact

89 between perovskite and MoO3 to be degraded, even compared

90 to samples without hole transport layer. The result is attributed

91 to

92 • the chemical reaction in the MoO3 ﬁlm at the very

93 interface, and

94 • an inadequate electronic level alignment between the two

95 layers.

96 To discriminate between these issues, we introduce an

97 ultrathin buﬀer layer (few nm) of 2,2′,7,7′-tetrakis(N,N-di-p-

98 methoxyphenyl-amine)-9,9′-spirobi-ﬂuorene (spiro-MeOTAD)

99 sandwiched between the perovskite and the MoO3 layer, which

100 inhibits the chemical reaction, and we investigate the inﬂuence

101 on the photovoltaic activity of the device.

132 Further insight in the energy level alignment at the

133 perovskite/oxide interface is gained from XPS data. Upon

134 deposition of increasing amounts of MoO3, both the iodine and

135 lead core levels (I 3d5/2 and Pb 4f7/2) of the perovskite layer

136 shift to lower binding energies (Figure 1d, e), by a total of 0.5

137 eV after deposition of 20 Å MoO3. This rigid shift indicates a

138 MoO3-induced band bending in the perovskite ﬁlm, consistent

139 with the deposition of the high work function oxide. The spin−

140 orbit split components of the Mo 3d core level do not exhibit

141 any signiﬁcant shift (Figure 1f). However, the decomposition of

142 the core level spectrum into components corresponding to

143 Mo6+, Mo5+, and Mo4+ oxidation states, with Mo 3d5/2 binding

144 energies at 233.2 eV, 232.0 and 230.1 eV respectively, reveals a

145 distinct component of substoichiometric molybdenum oxide.

146 While the presence of Mo6+ and Mo5+ has been seen repeatedly

147 for evaporated molybdenum oxide ﬁlms,12,20 the appearance of

148 the Mo4+ component (inset in Figure 1f), normally associated

149 with MoO2, is surprising. This Mo4+ contribution is only

150 apparent at very low ﬁlm thickness (1.5 and 5 Å in Figure 1f),

151 which indicates that the pronounced reduction to molybdenum

152 dioxide is constrained to the MAPbI3/oxide interface and likely

153 involves the perovskite layer.

154 In order to suppress this interface chemical reaction, a 35 Å

155 thick buﬀer layer of the hole transport material spiro-MeOTAD

156 was evaporated on top of the perovskite ﬁlm, as a means to

157 protect the absorber from the subsequently evaporated MoO3.

158 The thickness of the buﬀer layer was thick enough to prevent

159 direct physical contact between the perovskite and the oxide,

160 yet thin enough to maintain good electronic transport through

161 the layer stack.

164 system. The secondary electron cutoﬀ(Figure 2a) shows that

176 coverage, the electronic structure in the valence band region

177 evolves with the appearance of the unperturbed Mo 4d level.

178 Beyond 20 Å, the spectrum is indistinguishable from that of the

180 MeOTAD buﬀer layer.

182 the Pb 4f and I 3d levels observed for the system without spiro-

183 MeOTAD. However, in contrast to the previous case, the Mo

184 3d core level does not exhibit any signiﬁcant Mo4+ component

185 (inset of Figure 2f), indicating that the spiro-MeOTAD layer

186 fulﬁlls its role of a buﬀer layer and prevents the chemical

187 reaction at the perovskite/molybdenum oxide interface, and

188 thus the formation of MoO2.

189 The region of the valence band close to EF comprises a

190 complex spectral superposition of various components. In the

191 system without the spiro-MeOTAD interlayer, a DOS appears

192 at 0.2 eV below the Fermi level with the initial deposition of

193 one monolayer of molybdenum oxide (Figure 1c). MoO2 has

194 been reported in the literature to be metallic with EF cutting

195 through the 4d bands.21 This picture changes with the

196 application of the spiro-MeOTAD buﬀer layer on MAPbI3.

197 The HOMO onset of the organic HTM is at ∼1.0 eV below EF 198 prior to MoO3 deposition (Figure 2c). The subsequently

199 evaporated oxide layer p-dopes the spiro-MeOTAD, and the

200 HTM HOMO onset shifts to 0.6 eV below EF, with a tail of

201 states reaching almost up to the Fermi level for a 1.5 Å MoO3 202 overlayer thickness. Note that the same coverage of 1.5 Å of

203 MoO3 on bare MAPbI3 led to the formation of an interface

204 state (IS) originating from reduced MoO2 (Figure 1c).

205 Eventually, with 20 Å of deposited molybdenum oxide, the

206 electronic structure of the MoO3 surface, as it is also found for

207 the system without spiro-MeOTAD interlayer, is recovered.

208 The combined results from the PES measurements are

209 summarized in the energy level diagrams of the interface with

f3 210 and without the spiro-MeOTAD buﬀer layer (Figure 3). The

211 shift of the Pb 4f and I 3d core levels is the same without

212 (Figures 1d, e) and with (Figures 2d, e) the buﬀer layer, and

213 indicates a 0.5 eV band bending induced in the perovskite layer

214 by the deposition of MoO3. This 0.5 eV shift of the perovskite

215 VBM (and core levels) toward EF is neither enhanced nor

216 impeded by the reduced MoO2 found in the spiro-MeOTAD-

217 free device, and seems therefore to originate solely from the

218 electrostatic potential imposed by the high work function of the

219 molybdenum oxide layer. Information on how far the band

220 bending reaches into the perovskite layer is diﬃcult to obtain,

221 and it is assumed here that the ﬁlm remains n-type, i.e., EF close

222 to the conduction band minimum, at and near the interface

223 with the bottom TiO2 substrate. Previous studies have

224 demonstrated that the Fermi level position in hybrid organic

225 lead halide perovskites is strongly inﬂuenced by the doping

226 character and work function of the (oxide) substrate,5,22 i.e.,

227 perovskite ﬁlms deposited on TiO2 have n-type character while

228 those deposited on NiO have a slight p-type character. This

229 adaptive change of the Fermi level position as a function of the

230 electronic properties of the substrate also implies a very low

231 density of deep electronic levels in the perovskite band gap and

232 low doping concentrations.23,24 We therefore assume that the

233 MAPbI3 ﬁlm sandwiched between TiO2 and MoO3 gradually

234 changes from n-type to intrinsic, as depicted in Figure 3.

235 The electronic structure of these interfaces is expected to

236 aﬀect solar cell functionality and performance. In particular,

237 band bending and a corresponding internal ﬁeld could alter

238 carrier transport through the perovskite ﬁlm and change

239 recombination rates. Furthermore, the role of the chemistry at

240 the perovskite/MoO3 interface on charge carrier collection

241 needs to be characterized in detail. To test the respective

242 impact of MoO3 and spiro-MeOTAD/MoO3 interlayers on

243 device characteristics, we use copper(II) phthalocyanine

244 (CuPc) as our choice for a hole transport layer, since it can

245 be evaporated on top of the designed hole extraction layers

246 without redissolving the single constituents of that junction,

247 such as the undoped spiro-MeOTAD (u-spiro-MeOTAD)

248 buﬀer layer. Previous studies showed that CuPc can be used

249 reasonably well as HTM in perovskite solar cells even though

250 the expected eﬃciencies are lower than for devices with a

251 standard doped spiro-MeOTAD (d-spiro-MeOTAD) HTL.25

252 Furthermore, the energy alignment of the CuPc HOMO level

253 with the MAPbI3 VBM has been found to be similar to that of

254 spiro-MeOTAD.26 We therefore produced the following three

255 solar cell conﬁgurations: glass/FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3/MoO3/

256 CuPc/Au, glass/FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3/CuPc/Au, and glass/

257 FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3/u-spiro-MeOTAD/MoO3/CuPc/Au, re-

258 spectively. The undoped spiro-MeOTAD interlayer is spin-

259 coated from a dilute solution to yield a ﬁlm thickness ≤5 nm.

260 According to the photoemission experiments, any MoO3 261 thickness above 20 Å leads to a ﬁlm with a work function

262 larger than 5.5 eV. Thus, a layer thickness of 35 Å is used here

263 to induce maximum band bending without signiﬁcantly

264 increasing the series resistance (cf. Figure 3 and Figure S3),

363 Tracking of the maximum power point output has been

364 conducted in accordance to earlier reports (see Figure S1).31

365 The EQE curves presented in Figure 4b show that major

366 losses occur for carriers generated with longer wavelength

367 photons for the devices with MoO3 and u-spiro-MeOTAD/

368 MoO3 interlayer. This observation can be attributed to two

369 distinct eﬀects. First, it is another indication for increased

370 probability of recombination close to the hole extraction

371 contact in devices with interlayer, as the blue light is absorbed

372 predominantly near the electron-extracting TiO2 contact.

373 Second, in devices with the high-work-function hole extraction

374 contact, charge collection at that side of the cell is reduced

375 which can potentially be linked to the band bending induced in

376 the perovskite layer by the high work function of the adjacent

377 MoO3 charge extraction layer. In this picture the collection at

378 the MAPbI3/u-spiro-MeOTAD/MoO3/CuPc junction would

379 be particularly reduced. Although devices with only the thin u-

380 spiro-MeOTAD layer but without MoO3 layer between the

381 MAPbI3 and CuPc exhibit the same performance parameters as

382 devices with a direct MAPbI3/CuPc junction (see Figure S5),

383 the u-spiroMeOTAD/MoO3/CuPc system is detrimental for

384 unimpeded hole transfer. Essentially the u-spiro-MeOTAD and

385 CuPc become p-doped by the n-type MoO3 layer (Figure S4)

386 in the interface region, which leads to band bending in the

387 CuPc ﬁlm. In consequence, hole transport toward the top

388 electrode occurs against the ﬁeld in the CuPc layer and is

389 therefore deteriorated.

390 Photoluminescence spectroscopy measurements were per-

391 formed in order to further investigate the collection of charges

392 that are photogenerated in the perovskite absorber. Here, the

393 decay time of the characteristic photoluminescence emission

394 f5 (Figure 5) observed at 770 nm wavelength can serve as a proxy

395 to track the fate of photoexcited carriers in the device structures

396 with varied HTL conﬁguration. Only small diﬀerences in carrier

397 quenching can be observed between the MAPbI3 with an

398 immediate CuPc, MoO3/CuPc, or u-spiro-MeOTAD/MoO3/

399 CuPc HTL interface. A double exponential ﬁt to the decay

400 curves reveals initial fast recombination with time constants τ1 401 of 3 ns for all three ﬁlms followed by a second order decay time

402 τ2 which amounts to 19, 12, and 17 ns, respectively. This

403 indicates that interface recombination is slightly increased for

404 the samples with an immediate MAPbI3/MoO2 interface, which

405 can in part be mitigated by introducing the thin u-spiro-

406 MeOTAD interlayer. The emission spectra depicted in Figure

407 5b of the three diﬀerent samples look virtually identical, which

408 leads to the conclusion that this increased interface

409 recombination does not open new radiative decay channels.

410 In summary, the results from these time-resolved photo-

411 luminescence measurements indicate that the observed changes

412 in the interfacial electronic structure do not strongly contribute

413 to recombination and carrier quenching in the MAPbI3 bulk.

414 This is in contrast to reports of alternative charge carrier

415 extraction interlayers (e.g., carbon nanotubes) in which changes

418 In conclusion, our study demonstrates that the evaporation

419 of MoO3 on top of a TiO2/MAPbI3 ﬁlm induces band bending

420 in the perovskite ﬁlm, which as a result of this, becomes nearly

421 intrinsic at the MAPbI3/MoO3 interface. However, the

422 molybdenum oxide layer is reduced to MoO2 at the very

423 interface, indicative of a chemical reaction with the perovskite,

424 which leads to a decline in device performance partially due to a

425 small increase in interface recombination. Introducing a

426 protective buﬀer layer, such as a very thin ﬁlm of spiro-

427 MeOTAD, inhibits the chemical reaction between the oxide

428 and the absorber and mitigates some of the interface

429 recombination while maintaining the band bending in the

430 perovskite, driven by the high work function of the oxide.

431 However, despite the band bending in the perovskite being

432 nominally favorable for charge collection, both conﬁgurations

433 lead to an unusual yet very signiﬁcant impairment of device

434 characteristics, which needs to be considered for the design of

435 hybrid perovskite-based electronics.

436■EXPERIMENTAL SECTION

437 Film Preparation. Fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) covered glass 438 substrates were cleaned by sequential sonication in aqueous alconox 439 solution, deionized water, acetone and ethanol for 15 min each and 440 subsequently dried in a N2 stream. The compact-TiO2 (100 nm) was 441 then applied to the substrate in a spray pyrolysis process using a 20 442 mM solution of titanium diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate) in 443 isopropanol and air as carrier gas. Substrates were held at 350 °C 444 on a hot plate during spray pyrolysis, and subsequently annealed at 445 500 °C for 1 h in air. 446 CH3NH3I was synthesized by mixing methyl amine (40% in 447 methanol) with concentrated HI acid in a 1:1 molar ratio under 448 continuous stirring at 0 °C for 2 h. CH3NH3I was then crystallized in a 449 rotary evaporator, washed in diethyl ether and ﬁltered. Eventually, the 450 crystals were dried overnight in vacuo at 60 °C. 451 In the subsequent step, a 0.84 M solution of MAPbI3 was prepared 452 in an N2-ﬁlled glovebox by mixing PbCl2 and CH3NH3I in a 1:3 molar 453 ratio in N, N-dimethylformamide. The solution was heated to 60 °C 454 and stirred until a clear yellow solution was formed. For the coating 455 process the solution taken out of the glovebox and transferred into a 456 drybox with controlled humidity (%RH = 20 ± 5). The solution was 457 spin-coated in two stages: 5 s at 500 r.p.m. and then at 1,500 r.p.m. for 458 40 s. The substrate was then heated on a hot plate set at 120 °C for 60 459 min, after which the substrate turned deep black in color. 460 MAPbI3-covered substrates were always kept under inert atmos- 461 phere and loaded into an ultrahigh vacuum chamber for PES 462 measurements and deposition of molybdenum oxide. MoO3 (powder, 463 Molybdenum(VI) oxide, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.98%) was thermally 464 evaporated in a vacuum chamber operated at a base pressure <1 × 465 10−8 Torr a rate of 0.05 Å/s monitored on a quartz crystal 466 microbalance. The thin spiro-MeOTAD interlayer was evaporated 467 from a Knudsen cell in the same vacuum system at a rate of 0.02 Å/s. 468 More details on the evaporation of spiro-MeOTAD layers and the 469 respective electronic properties of the ﬁlm can be found in the work of 470 Ono et al.34

471 Photoemission Spectroscopy. Photoemission experiments were 472 performed in a custom built UHV chamber with in situ sample transfer 473 between measurement position and MoO3 deposition compartment. 474 UPS spectra were acquired from He I (21.22 eV) and He II (40.8 eV) 475 excitation lines at a nominal experimental resolution below 150 meV. 476 XPS spectra were taken using Al Kα radiation (1486.7 eV) at a 477 resolution of 800 meV. The acquired spectra were calibrated to the 478 Fermi edge of a sputter-cleaned Au surface. 479 Device Fabrication. Prepatterned FTO substrates (Thin Film 480 Devices) were cleaned by sonication in acetone and 2-propanol prior 481 to 15 min of UV ozone cleaning. A compact TiO2 layer was deposited

482 by spin-coating a 0.15 M titanium diisopropoxide dis(acetylacetonate)

483 (Sigma-Aldrich, 75% (w/w) in isopropanol) in 1-butanol (Sigma-

484 Aldrich, 99.8%) solution at 700 rpm for 10 s, 1000 rpm for 10 s and

485 2000 rpm for 30 s. The compact layer was dried on a hot plate at 125

486 °C for >5 min. The mesoporous TiO2 (mp-TiO2) layer was deposited

487 from a solution consisting of 60 mg of commercial 30 nm TiO2 488 nanoparticle paste (Dyesol, 30 NR-D) diluted in 1 mL of ethanol, and

489 spin-coated at 700 rpm for 10 s, 1000 rpm for 10 s, and 2000 rpm for 490 30 s. The ﬁlms were sintered at 500 °C for 1 h.

491 The CH3NH3PbI3 photoactive layer was deposited by a procedure

492 reported by Ahn et al.35 The precursor solution consisted of 461 mg of

493 PbI2, 159 mg of CH3NH3I, and 78 mg of DMSO (molar ratio 1:1:1) in

494 600 mg of DMF. The solution was stirred at room temperature until

495 fully dissolved and then passed through a 0.45 μm PTFE syringe ﬁlter

496 prior to use. To deposit the CH3NH3PbI3 ﬁlm, the precursor solution

497 was spin-coated on top of the mp-TiO2 ﬁlm at 4000 rpm for 25 s.

498 While the substrate was rotating (after spinning at 4000 rpm for

499 approximately 10 s), 0.5 mL of diethyl ether was dripped onto to the

500 substrate in a continuous stream. The resultant transparent ﬁlm was

501 heated at 65 °C for 1 min and 100 °C for 2 min in order to obtain a

502 highly specular CH3NH3PbI3 ﬁlm. The d-spiro-OMeTAD layer for

503 control devices was deposited by spin-coating a solution containing 72

504 mg spiro-OMeTAD (Lumtec), 28.8 uL 4-tert-butylpyridine,17.5 μL of

505 LiTFSI stock solution (stock: 520 mg mL−1 LiTFSI in acetonitrile), 506 and 1 mL chlorobenzene at 5000 rpm for 30 s.

507 The MoO3 was deposited on MAPbI3 and MAPIbI3/u-spiro-

508 OMeTAD at a rate of 0.2 Å/s at a base pressure lower than 2 × 10−7

509 Torr for a total thickness of 3.5 nm.

510 CuPc hole transport layers were evaporated in an Angstrom

511 Evaporator setup at a base pressure of 1 × 10−8 mbar and deposition

512 rate of 0.5 Å/s monitored on a quartz crystal microbalance. Films of

513 incremental thicknesses (2, 5, 10, and 20 nm) on top of the MAPbI3 514 and MAPbI3/MoO3 ﬁlms were transferred with a brief (<5 min)

515 exposure to ambient atmosphere to a separate vacuum chamber to

516 perform analysis of the energy level evolution by photoemission

517 spectroscopy or to a remote metallization chamber to ﬁnalize device

518 production. For the devices, Au electrodes were deposited through a

519 shadow mask at a rate ranging from 0.5 to 2 Å/s for a total thickness of 520 100 nm.

521 Device Measurements. The J−V characteristics for six devices in

522 each device geometry were measured with a Keithley 2450-LV

523 SourceMeter and controlled with an Igor-based, in-house designed

524 program. The scan direction was set from +1.5 V to −0.5 V, with 0.01

525 V steps, and a scan rate of 0.225 V/s. A solar simulator (Newport,

526 Oriel Sol3A) equipped with an AM1.5 ﬁlter and calibrated with an

527 NREL certiﬁed Si photodiode was used for illumination. The EQE was

528 measured with a Newport Oriel IQE-200 with a chopping frequency of 529 60 Hz.

530 Photoluminescence Measurements. Time resolved photo-

531 luminescence was measured using a Hamamatsu streak camera system

532 (C10910−05), whereas the excitation source was a Fianium

533 Supercontinuum high power broadband ﬁber laser (SC400−2-PP).

534 The chosen excitation wavelength was 530 nm at ∼25 μW power on a

535 spot size of 0.02 mm2. The decay curve of PL emission was ﬁtted using 536 a single exponential model.
